analysis.one_liner: Waves the government's royalties on new deepwater Gulf of Mexico oil and gas production.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill; it sat in committee and was set aside in favor of a Senate companion bill, so its royalty exemptions never became law through this measure.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let oil and gas companies take oil and gas from deep water in the federal Gulf of Mexico without paying royalties — the public's share of the value of what's extracted — until each lease produced a large set volume (as much as 87.5 million barrels of oil equivalent in the deepest water). It would also require royalty-free production for new leases sold in those waters over the next five years. Royalties would come back only if oil topped $28 a barrel or natural gas topped $3.50 per million BTU.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies holding or buying deepwater Gulf of Mexico leases, mostly large oil producers. They would sell millions of barrels from federal waters and keep the share normally paid to the federal government — for example, the first 87.5 million barrels of oil equivalent from any lease in water deeper than 800 meters would be royalty-free.

how_it_helps.text: For existing leases in Gulf water depths of 200 meters or more, no royalty payments would be due on new production until set volumes were reached: at least 17.5 million barrels of oil equivalent in 200–400 meters of water, 52.5 million in 400–800 meters, and 87.5 million in deeper water.
For any new lease sales in those waters within five years of enactment, the bill would require the bidding system to include royalty suspensions at no less than those same minimum volumes.
The bill would also give the Interior Secretary broad authority to reduce or eliminate royalties or net profit shares on existing leases to promote development or increased production.
The bill's stated purpose is national energy security through encouraging domestic deepwater production.

Royalties return at the lease rate during any year in which average oil prices exceed $28 per barrel or average natural gas prices exceed $3.50 per million BTU, with the thresholds adjusted for inflation.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers. Royalties are the public's share of the value of oil and gas taken from federally owned waters; every royalty-free barrel is revenue the Treasury does not collect. Federal programs that receive mineral royalties would also get less.

drawbacks.text: The bill converts public royalty revenue into extra profit for some of the largest energy companies; the exemption applies to leases in federal waters, where the oil belongs to the public and royalties are how the public gets paid for it.

The volume thresholds are set in the bill itself, so once the Secretary finds production would not be economic without relief, no royalties are due on as much as 87.5 million barrels of oil equivalent from a single deepwater lease regardless of later profitability.

The bill gives oil companies until 1995 price levels as the baseline: royalties return only if oil averages above $28 per barrel or gas above $3.50 per million BTU, thresholds the bill itself adjusts only for inflation.
The Secretary's decisions on royalty relief would be final agency action, reviewable in court only if a suit is filed within 30 days, limiting outside challenge.

The good-faith case for it: deepwater drilling was then expensive and financially risky at prevailing prices, and supporters argued relief was needed to keep development in the Gulf rather than overseas.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs are concrete and the benefits speculative. The bill hands a specified, quantified quantity of public mineral revenue to a concentrated industry, while the public benefits only indirectly — through possible increases in domestic production and energy security that the bill assumes rather than guarantees. Its own price triggers, which reinstate royalties at $28 oil and $3.50 gas, are an acknowledgment by its drafters that at then-current prices the relief is a straight transfer.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, and it never came back for a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. W.J. (Billy) Tauzin of Louisiana introduced the bill on July 25, 1995, joined by 18 cosponsors (13 Republicans and 5 Democrats).

The House referred it to the Natural Resources Committee on July 25, 1995, and to that committee's Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee on July 31; the committee also asked the Interior Department for its comments.
On November 28, 1995, the record notes 'See S.395,' the Senate companion bill, and no further action was taken on the House bill.
The bill was never reported out of committee and never received a floor vote in the House before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, no royalty exemption was created through this measure and the Treasury continued to collect royalties on deepwater Gulf leases as they existed; oil companies did not gain the relief this bill would have provided, though the Senate companion remained the vehicle for the same idea.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The Treasury kept collecting the royalties

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including members from Texas and Louisiana Gulf Coast districts.

against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill out of committee, keeping it from a House vote.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, so no opposition is on the record; sponsorship leaned Republican (13 of 18 cosponsors) but included 5 Democrats, and the Gulf Coast delegation was bipartisan.

industries.industry: Deepwater oil and gas producers (Gulf of Mexico)
industries.note: The bill exempts new deepwater production from royalties — the public's share of oil taken from federal waters — worth millions to tens of millions of dollars per lease. The industry's gain is directly the Treasury's lost revenue.

industries.industry: Offshore drilling and oilfield service contractors
industries.note: By lowering the cost of deepwater development, royalty relief would encourage more Gulf projects, generating drilling and service work. The benefit is indirect and depends on companies proceeding with development.
A royalty-free deepwater production channel would put shallower leases, which still owe royalties, at a competitive disadvantage. No relief was offered for them in the bill.
